entities.name: Antigonus II Gonatas
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Antigonus II Gonatas, King of Macedon from 276 BCE until his death in 239 BCE, was the architect of the Antigonid dynasty's enduring power in the Hellenistic world following decades of instability after the death of Alexander the Great. His reign marked a crucial period for Macedonian hegemony over Greece, establishing a balance of power with rival Hellenistic kingdoms like the Ptolemaic and Seleucid empires, and profoundly influencing the political landscape of the Aegean for nearly four decades. He inherited a kingdom ravaged by the Wars of the Diadochi and the recent Celtic invasions, transforming it into a formidable regional power and a center of Hellenistic culture and philosophy.

His most celebrated achievement was the decisive victory over the invading Gauls (Celts) at the Battle of Lysimachia around 277 BCE, which secured Macedon's northern borders and earned him immense prestige among the Greek city-states. This triumph allowed him to consolidate his authority, leading to his proclamation as king. He then engaged in a series of conflicts, notably the Chremonidean War (267–261 BCE) against an alliance of Athens and Sparta, supported by Ptolemaic Egypt, which reaffirmed Macedonian control over central and southern Greece. He also fought naval battles, including the Battle of Cos (c. 255 BCE) against the Ptolemaic fleet, asserting Macedonian maritime influence in the Aegean. His strategic alliances, particularly with the Aetolian League, helped maintain a fragile peace and order within the fragmented Hellenistic world.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Antigonus II Gonatas's reign solidified the Antigonid dynasty, ensuring Macedonian stability and influence in the Hellenistic world for another century. His victory over the Gauls and strategic leadership prevented further fragmentation of the Greek mainland.
